# hdtp-identity — the contract every port implements

One library, several homes: a Rust core (`crates/hdtp-identity`) compiled to WebAssembly for the
browser, Cloudflare Workers and Node (`crates/hdtp-identity-wasm`, loaders in `js/`), compiled
natively for the `hdtp` CLI (`crates/hdtp`), and an independent Go port (`go/`) that the vectors tie
to the first. This file is the boundary all of them present: **bytes in, JSON out**, no state, the
same names, the same shapes. The specification is hdtp-spec's `docs/specification/` (1.0.0) and, where
the spec leaves a byte to the implementer, `hdtp-spec/vectors/lib/*.mjs` — the seed library —
which every port must match byte for byte on the vectors in
`hdtp-spec/vectors/hdtp-1.0-vectors.json` and in the specification's Appendix B.

**This file is generated.** `contract/contract.json` is the source: 55 functions, each with
the shape of its arguments, the shape of its answer and the error codes it may fail with, over the
domain types they are assembled from. `js/parity.mjs` validates every answer of BOTH ports against
that same file, so these tables and the gate cannot describe different contracts — which they did:
the tables said `card_decode` answers with a `leaf` while one port had stopped sending one, and said
nothing at all about `decide`'s `tool`, which was `null` in Rust and absent in Go. The prose around
the tables is `contract/CONTRACT.template.md` and is written by hand.

## 0. Conventions

- **Bytes in JSON** are base64url without padding (`b64url`), and an answer always spells them so.
  An argument's bytes are read forgiving the padding and the standard alphabet's `+` and `/`, and
  nothing else: whitespace of any kind, any other character outside the alphabet, `=` anywhere but
  the end, and a last character with a spare bit set are `{"error": "parse", "why": "not
  base64url"}`. Every string a port reads that it did not write itself — a card's certificate, a
  chain in a peer's plaintext, a pin's leaf, a held key, a vault's salt, nonce and ciphertext — is
  read by the same rule and refused in its function's words. One step comes first for a card's
  certificate alone: its value loses every space, tab, CR and LF, which a fold or a paste puts there
  (SPEC §3, *Reading a card*; `card_decode`). One list of cases,
  `js/b64url-arguments.json`, holds both ports to it. The members of an envelope that travelled are
  read by a stricter rule (§5). The vector file alone uses hex.
- **Instants** in JSON are RFC 3339 UTC strings with second precision (`"2026-09-13T12:00:00Z"`);
  `ts` and `exp` inside an envelope header stay integer Unix seconds, as the spec says.
- **Keys**: a private key is PKCS #8 DER; a public key is SubjectPublicKeyInfo DER. Algorithms are
  `"ed25519"` and `"p256"`. A **fingerprint** is `"sha256:" + b64url(SHA-256(SPKI))`; a **key id** is
  the 32 raw bytes of that hash. A key of any other algorithm — RSA, P-384, a bare X25519 key, an
  Ed25519 key whose AlgorithmIdentifier carries parameters — is refused where it is read, as a key or
  inside a certificate or a request: `{"error": "unsupported", "why": "unsupported key type <OID>"}`,
  the OID the key's AlgorithmIdentifier names first (a function that answers a refusal as its result
  carries the same words: chain rule 1, `csr_check`, `card_decode`). The seed's `parse` refuses it in
  the same words, a P-256 key whose curve OID has a padded subidentifier included, and reads a
  SubjectPublicKeyInfo as the ports do: `SubjectPublicKeyInfo shape` for anything but its
  AlgorithmIdentifier and a key BIT STRING with no unused bits, `P-256 key is not a point` for one off
  the curve (hdtp-spec b841dd3; before it the seed named these in OpenSSL's words or as an OID not
  in the DER form, and read a key with unused bits).
- **Every function returns one JSON object.** Success shapes are listed per function. Failure is
  `{"error": "<code>", "why": "<one line>"}`, where `code` is one of the contract's `ErrorCode`
  (`bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported`, `envelope_invalid`, `vault`, `root_expired`, `key`, `internal`), and each function lists the codes it can fail with, which `js/parity.mjs` holds
  both ports to. `chain_required`, `certificate_renewed` and `pending_approval` are not failures: they
  are the `code` of an answer of `decide` (§5.1), which succeeds. Ports never throw across the
  boundary.
- **A member that is absent is not a member that is empty.** Absent answers `{"error": "bad_request",
  "why": "<name> is required"}` naming the member the caller left out; present but unusable — `""`,
  bytes that will not decode, a string where an object belongs — answers what is wrong with the value
  (`parse`/`"not base64url"`, a parser's own words). A port whose zero value and missing value are
  the same thing loses this distinction, and both have: `{"spki": ""}` once read as "spki is
  required" in one port and as a truncated DER in the other. The JSON literal `null` counts as absent.
- **A member of the wrong JSON type is refused, never read as absent** — an optional one too, which is
  where the ports parted: one read `"serial": 7` as no serial and drew a random one, `"guest": "yes"`
  as not a guest and `"exp": "7"` as ts + 600, and the other refused each. A base64url member that is
  not a string answers `{"error": "parse", "why": "not base64url"}`, as bytes that will not decode
  do; any other answers `bad_request` in words that name it — `<name> is required`, the words its
  absence gets, unless the function has more particular ones (`first_line is a line number from 1`).
  An integer is a number written without a fraction or an exponent, and not `-0`: `365.0` and `-0`
  are not a number of days, although JavaScript reads both as one.
- **The order a function reads its members is part of its answer.** When several required members are
  missing, the one named is the first the function needs, and both ports read them in the same order.
- **A member a function does not declare is refused**, before any member is read: `{"error":
  "bad_request", "why": "<fn> takes no member \"<m>\""}`, naming the first such member in sorted
  order. A function declares the members its `params` list, and no others. That holds the arguments
  object. An object inside a member is read one of two ways, and both ports read each the same way
  (`js/parity.mjs` sends every object in every function's base an undeclared member, and requires a
  refusal of a document and an answer for the second kind, which `js/cases/generated.mjs`'s
  `READ_FOR_WHAT_IT_NEEDS` lists per function):
  - **a document** — something a port writes and a port reads back, whose members SPEC or this
    contract lists — is held to its members, and one it does not list is refused in its function's
    words: a vault document and its `kdf`; `wallet_issue`'s vault and record plaintexts and the roots,
    contacts and passkey inside them; a ledger entry; a signing request; `export_manifest`'s manifest,
    its `counts` and `files`, and `hashes`; a row of `export_write`'s `contacts` and `threads` and of
    `export_write_messages`'s `messages`; a wallet contact of `book_rows`; the limits rules and a
    charge;
  - **what a host hands in of its own state, or of what a peer sent it** — an envelope, a node state
    and its keys and pins, a pin, the answer to `get_card` and its `data`, a directory entry,
    `export_merge`'s held pins and rows, `export_write`'s media — and the JSON a seal carries
    (`vault_seal`'s plaintext, of which only `v` is read, `seal_request`'s `params`, `seal_result`'s
    `result`) are read for the members they need and not held to their schemas'
    `additionalProperties`: a host's typed port decodes them into fixed structs and cannot see a
    member it has no field for either.
- **`why` is part of the answer.** Two ports refusing the same call in different words is a
  divergence, not a detail: it is what a person debugging reads, and what a caller's test asserts. No
  `why` may be a library's own error text — one port cannot reproduce another library's wording.
- **The name is judged first.** A name no function has answers `{"error": "unsupported", "why": "no
  function named <name>"}`, whatever the arguments are — a list, `null`, text that does not parse, or
  any of what the next two rules refuse. Everything below is judged only for a function that exists.
- **Half a surrogate pair is refused next, before the arguments are read.** Arguments holding a `\u`
  escape of half a UTF-16 surrogate pair (a high one not followed by a low one, or a low one alone)
  answer `{"error": "bad_request", "why": "args: a string holds half of a UTF-16 surrogate pair"}`
  from every function: one JSON parser refuses such text and another reads it as U+FFFD, and a port
  must not answer by its parser's choice.
- **So is what one JSON parser refuses and another reads**, next: a number that is infinite as a
  double (`1e400`) answers `{"error": "bad_request", "why": "args: a number is outside the range of a
  double"}`, and arrays and objects nested more than 127 deep, the arguments object counted, `args:
  nested more than 127 deep` — whichever comes first in the text. JSON that travels as text — an
  envelope's header and body, a manifest, a line of `messages.jsonl`, a vault's plaintext — holding
  either, or half a surrogate pair, or a byte that is not UTF-8, is text that is not JSON, answered
  as each function answers that (a manifest or a line that is not UTF-8 is refused before it is read
  as JSON, as `not UTF-8 text`). RFC 8785, in which a
  header is written, has no infinite number. Arguments that do not parse at all answer `args is a
  JSON object`, and so do arguments with no text at all (Go's `Call(name, nil)` included): no
  arguments is `{}`, which the JS loader and the Go line adapter send for a call that gives none.
- **`version` is the one exception.** It describes the port, not a rule, so its answer differs and
  nothing compares it.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `version` | — | `spec`: string, `crate`?: string, `module`?: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | The build, not a rule: `spec` is the version of hdtp-spec's specification the port implements and is the same everywhere; the other member names the port's own release, so the answers differ and nothing compares them. |
- The Wasm boundary takes `&str` JSON and `&[u8]` DER and returns `String` JSON. The Go port exposes
  the same boundary as `Call(name, args)`, and most of the functions also as Go functions on
  `[]byte`/`string` returning structs; the export section is reached through `Call` alone, beside the
  two typed conveniences for a whole file, `ReadExportZip` and `WriteExportZip` (§6.2). It also builds a
  `hdtp-identity-go` binary that reads JSON requests on stdin, one per line (`{"fn": "<name>", "args":
  {...}}`), and writes one JSON answer per line, so the JavaScript suites can aim the same cases at
  both ports through one process per run.

| `key_from_seed` | `alg`: Alg, `seed`: Seed32 | `alg`: Alg, `pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | An Ed25519 seed is used directly; a P-256 scalar is the seed mod n, with 0 → 1 (the seed library's `keys.mjs`). Written for the vectors, and production API since SPEC §2.1: it is how a wallet turns a derived seed into its root. |
| `prf_salt` | — | `salt`: Seed32, `infos`: [string]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | SPEC §2.1's fixed PRF input, `SHA-256("hdtp/vault/1")`, and the three `info` strings. A call rather than a constant a caller copies, so the bytes live in one place and the vectors prove them. |
| `derive_seed` | `prf`: Seed32, `info`: string | `seed`: Seed32<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | `HKDF-SHA256(ikm = prf, salt = "", info, L = 32)`. **Refuses an `info` outside the three, and a `prf` that is not 32 bytes.** Both refusals are the point rather than hygiene: a mistyped domain separator would otherwise return 32 perfectly good bytes and silently derive an identity belonging to nobody, which is the one failure the derived-root design exists to prevent. |
| `public_key` | `pkcs8`: Pkcs8 | `alg`: Alg, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |

| `sign` | `pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `data`: B64url | `sig`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | Ed25519 pure, or ECDSA P-256/SHA-256 in ASN.1 DER, **always the low-S twin** (`s ≤ n/2`, SPEC §14.1): a library returns either twin of an ECDSA signature, and a port returns one. |

`sign` is the leaf key's one signing primitive; a host signs exactly four structures with it
(SPEC §13.5). The CLI exposes no signing command and no pass-through to `call`, so there is no other
use to make of it there — by omission, not by a guard: nobody should add an `hdtp sign` believing one
exists.

| `parse_certificate` | `der`: CertDer | `kind`: root\|leaf\|other, `subject`: string, `issuer`: string, `serial`: B64url, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant, `alg`: Alg, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint, `key_id`: B64url, `ski`: B64url \| null, `aki`: B64url \| null, `ca`: boolean, `path_len`: integer\|null, `key_usage`: [integer], `eku`: [string], `uris`: [string], `dns`: [string], `sig_alg`: string, `extensions`: [`id`: string, `critical`: boolean], `profile_error`: string\|null, `bytes`: integer<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | Parsing itself refuses, with a `parse` error, what DER has one encoding for and the certificate spells another way: the AlgorithmIdentifier inside the TBS differing from the one outside (`signature algorithm inside and outside differ`), a BOOLEAN that is not `0xFF` or is an explicit FALSE, a non-minimal INTEGER, an OBJECT IDENTIFIER with a padded subidentifier, a `keyUsage` BIT STRING whose unused bits are set or whose trailing zero bits are not removed, a validity of other than two times, an extension of other than two or three parts or whose value is not an OCTET STRING (`certificate shape`) or whose OCTET STRING holds more than one TLV, a P-256 key that is not the uncompressed point. A `keyUsage` BIT STRING with no initial octet (`03 00`; X.690 §8.6.2) is `BIT STRING not in the DER form`, and an `[3]` with nothing in it `not a v3 certificate with extensions`, in the seed and both ports. Both ports read a certificate's fields in one order, so one with two faults is named for the same one: the version, the serial, the validity's count, the outer algorithm's shape and its equality with the inner one, the key, the signature algorithm, the issuer, the subject, the two times, then the extensions, each extension's criticality before its OID. The seed's `parse` reads them in another order — the two algorithms' equality before the serial and the validity's count, and the key after the names and the two times — so there a certificate with two faults can be named for the other one. Nothing compares the seed's words for a certificate with two faults: each scenario carries one (R33's seed half, recorded here rather than changed). |

A refusal is an answer, not a failure of the call: `rule` says which one refused. Rule 4 refuses, in this order, `root has expired` (the clock past the root's `notAfter`), `leaf outside its validity`, `leaf longer than 398 days` and `leaf outlives the root`; it never reads the root's `notBefore`. |
| `compare_leaves` | `pinned`: CertDer, `presented`: CertDer | `order`: same\|newer\|superseded\|conflict<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |
| `is_normal_https` | `url`: string | `normal`: boolean<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | An IPv6 literal carries no zone id, in any spelling (`[fe80::1%eth0]`, `[2001:db8::1%25eth0]`): RFC 3986 has none, and the WHATWG parser the seed's `isNormalHttps` uses refuses a `%` inside the brackets. So `address_guard`, chain rule 5, `csr_check`, `ledger_check` and the export's endpoint column refuse one as not the normal form. |
| `address_guard` | `endpoint`: string, `self_endpoint`?: string, `guest`?: boolean | `ok`: true<br>or `ok`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | Refuses a host that is a loopback, link-local, private, unspecified or CGNAT literal (`localhost`, `*.localhost`, `127/8`, `10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/16`, `169.254/16`, `100.64/10`, `0.0.0.0`, `::1`, `::`, `fc00::/7`, `fe80::/10`, deprecated site-local `fec0::/10`, NAT64's local-use `64:ff9b:1::/48`), an IPv6 literal that EMBEDS such an IPv4 address — IPv4-mapped, IPv4-compatible `::/96`, NAT64 `64:ff9b::/96`, 6to4 `2002::/16` — because a translator dials the address inside (`[64:ff9b::7f00:1]` is loopback on a NAT64 network, and a literal has no name to resolve, so this is the whole guard), and, for a guest, an endpoint equal to `self_endpoint`. DNS resolution is the host's; `ip_is_private` is exposed so the host applies the same predicate to what it resolves. |
| `ip_is_private` | `ip`: string | `private`: boolean<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | The predicate `address_guard` applies to a literal host, for the host to apply to what it resolves. One leading `[` and one trailing `]` are dropped, as a URL writes an IPv6 host, and no more. An IPv6 literal with a zone id (`fe80::1%eth0`) is private whatever its address: a zone is an interface scope (RFC 4007 §6), which no global address carries. Text that is no address is not private: an empty zone, and a zone on an IPv4 address, are no address, as Go's `netip` reads them. |

Serial numbers: random 8 bytes by default; when `serial` is supplied it is used as given, which is
how the vectors reproduce (`serial = SHA-256("serial/" + label)[0..8]`). Times encode as UTCTime
before 2050 and GeneralizedTime from 2050; the root's `not_after` is `99991231235959Z` unless the
caller gives the end date its person chose (`build_root`, `root_tbs`).
Signature algorithm OIDs, extension order, criticality, key-usage bit encoding and every other byte
follow `x509.mjs` — the vector certificates must reproduce exactly from the same inputs.

The wallet's monotonic rule is the caller's: `not_before` = the later of (now − 1 h) and (previous
leaf's `not_before` + 1 s); the core enforces `not_after − not_before ≤ 398 d` and refuses otherwise.

## 3. Certificate signing requests (PKCS #10, SPEC §9)

A CSR is `CertificationRequest ::= SEQUENCE { certificationRequestInfo, signatureAlgorithm, signature }`
with an exact profile of its own: `version` 0; `subject` one UTF-8 `commonName`; the host's SPKI;
`attributes [0]` holding exactly one `extensionRequest` (`1.2.840.113549.1.9.14`) whose value is one
`subjectAltName` extension (non-critical) with exactly one URI and optionally one `dNSName` equal to
its host; the signature is by the CSR's own key with that key's own algorithm (proof of possession).
Strict DER, nothing trailing.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `csr_new` | `cn`: string, `host_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `endpoint`: string, `dns_name`?: string | `der`: Csr<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |
| `csr_check` | `der`: Csr, `root_spkis`?: [Spki] | `ok`: true, `cn`: string, `spki`: Spki, `fingerprint`: Fingerprint, `alg`: Alg, `endpoint`: string, `dns_name`: string\|null<br>or `ok`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | Refuses a bad signature (no proof of possession), a key equal to any root in `root_spkis` (the root-key refusal), an endpoint that is not normal https, an endpoint the address guard refuses. `root_spkis` absent is no roots; present and unreadable is an error, never "no roots to refuse against". |
| `issue_from_csr` | `csr`: Csr, `root_cert`: CertDer, `root_spkis`?: [Spki], `now`: InstantIn, `previous_not_before`?: InstantIn, `valid_days`?: integer, `root_pkcs8`: Pkcs8 | `der`: CertDer, `endpoint`: string, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant, `warnings`: [string]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported`, `root_expired` | Read in this order: `now`; `root_cert`, judged before anything is signed — not a certificate, `parse`; not a root of the profile, `bad_request` `root_cert is not a root of the profile: <why>`; not self-signed, `bad_request` `root_cert is not self-signed`; past its `notAfter` at `now` (RFC 5280's inclusive reading), `root_expired` `the root ended at <instant>: it signs nothing more`; then `root_pkcs8`, which must be the certificate's key (`bad_request` `root_pkcs8 is not the key of root_cert`, after the request is checked); then `root_spkis`, then `csr_check` with the issuing root added to `root_spkis`, then `previous_not_before` and `valid_days`, and the leaf under the monotonic rule. `valid_days` absent is 365; an explicit 0 is refused. A leaf ends no later than its root (SPEC §14.2 rule 4): where the validity asked would run past the root's `notAfter`, `not_after` is the root's and `warnings` says `the leaf ends with its root, at <instant>: sooner than the validity asked`; otherwise `warnings` is empty. A `not_before` the monotonic rule puts after the root's `notAfter` is `root_expired` `the root ends at <instant>, before this leaf could begin`. |
| `issue_tbs_from_csr` | `csr`: Csr, `root_cert`: CertDer, `root_spkis`?: [Spki], `now`: InstantIn, `previous_not_before`?: InstantIn, `valid_days`?: integer | `tbs`: Tbs, `sig_alg`: SigAlg, `endpoint`: string, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant, `warnings`: [string]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported`, `root_expired` | As `issue_from_csr`, for the seam, with no `root_pkcs8`: the root's key signs `tbs` elsewhere, and `assemble_leaf` builds the leaf. An expired root is refused before a `tbs` exists, so nothing is ever put in front of a passkey or a card for it. |

### 3.1 Signing requests (SPEC §9.1)

A host asks a web wallet for a leaf with a form POSTed by top-level navigation, carrying a
`SigningRequest`: the CSR, `renew` or `move`, the root it expects, where the answer goes, an opaque
`state`, what the host calls itself, the validity it asks for, and when the request expires. The
wallet runs `signing_request_check` on it before a person sees anything, and answers by navigating
to `redirect` with `#chain=<leaf>.<root>&state=<state>` or `#error=<code>&state=<state>`. The
check is stateless: nothing of a request is kept.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `signing_request_check` | `request`: `{…}`, `origin`: string, `now`: InstantIn, `root_spkis`?: [Spki] | `ok`: true, `csr`: Csr, `redirect`: string, `purpose`: renew\|move, `valid_days`: integer<br>or `ok`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | What a web wallet decides about a host's signing request before a person sees it. The arguments first: `request` absent or not an object, `origin` absent or not a string, `now` absent (each `<name> is required`), `now` unreadable (`parse`), `root_spkis` unreadable — these are errors. Everything about the request itself is `{ok: false, why}`, the first thing wrong, in this order: a member a request does not carry (the first in sorted order: `a signing request does not carry <m>`); a member that is not a string (`<m> is a string, as a form carries it`) or over its bound (`<m> is longer than <n>`), in the order of SigningRequest's members; a required member absent or empty (`<m> is required`); an `origin` empty or `null` (`the request has no origin: a wallet answers only the origin that asked`); the redirect — not ASCII without spaces or backslashes (`the redirect is not an absolute URL`), a fragment (`the redirect carries a fragment`), not `https://` or `http://` (`the redirect is not https, or http to a loopback host`), userinfo (`the redirect carries userinfo`), a host not in lower-case normal form — IPv6 hex in lower case, a name of labels none of which is empty (`the redirect's host is not in normal form`), a port that is not 1–65535 without a leading zero (`the redirect's port is not in normal form`), `http` to a host that is not `localhost`, a dotted quad in `127.0.0.0/8` in normal form, or `[::1]` (`the redirect is not https, or http to a loopback host`); the redirect's origin (`scheme://host[:port]`, the default port left out) not equal to `origin` (`the redirect's origin is not the origin that asked`); `expires` not an RFC 3339 UTC instant in the one grammar — upper-case `T` and `Z`, `.` alone before a fraction (`expires is not an RFC 3339 instant`), not after `now` (`the request has expired`), or more than 600 seconds after it (`the request expires more than ten minutes ahead`); `purpose` not `renew` or `move` (`purpose is renew or move`; `signup` is not taken from a host); `valid_days` not a whole number 1–398 without a leading zero (`valid_days is a whole number of days from 1 to 398`); `state` not 43 base64url characters of 32 bytes (`state is 32 bytes, base64url`); `expect_root` not `sha256:` and 43 base64url characters (`expect_root is not a root fingerprint`); `root_cert`, when present, not base64url, not a certificate, not a root of §14.1's profile, or not the root `expect_root` names; `csr` not base64url (`csr is not base64url`); then `csr_check` with `root_spkis`, whose refusal is answered in its words. What stays the wallet's: proving the root against `expect_root` (§2.2), showing the asking origin, the `recipient` as the host's claim, the endpoint, the validity and whether the host is new, and the validity the person chooses. Nothing of the request is kept. |

## 4. Cards (SPEC §3)

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `card_encode` | `fn`: string, `cert`: CertDer, `seal`?: string, `extra`?: [string] | `vcard`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | Folded per RFC 6350 at 75 octets, CRLF, exactly as the seed's `card.mjs`. `extra` present and not a list of strings — a list holding a number or a `null`, or a value that is not a list — is `extra is required`, §0's words for a member of the wrong type. Refuses `<fn|seal|extra> carries a control character`: a card is lines, and a line break in anything a caller supplies writes a property of the caller's choosing (SPEC §3). |
| `card_decode` | `vcard`: string, `now`: InstantIn | `fn`: string, `version`: 1, `seal`: string, `cert`: CertDer, `root`: Fingerprint, `endpoint`: string, `expired`: boolean, `ignored`: [string], `bytes`: integer, `leaf`: Certificate<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | Every refusal of a card is `bad_request` with the exact `why` strings of `card.mjs`. A `now` that is not an instant is `parse`, `not an RFC 3339 instant: <now>`, as every function that reads an instant answers it (`""` included). An empty `X-HDTP-VERSION` names no version (`no X-HDTP-VERSION`). A card is read by SPEC §3's *Reading a card*, as `card.mjs` reads it: RFC 6350 unfolding (a CRLF or LF followed by one space or tab removed), then `X-HDTP-CERT` takes every following line that does not start a property (`[group.]NAME[;params]:`, the group and name of ASCII letters, digits and `-`), blank lines included, and loses every space, tab, CR and LF; any other line that starts no property is ignored. So a card whose folding a paste damaged reads. What is left is read as every string a port did not write is read (§0), so a stray character, any other whitespace (a vertical tab, a no-break space) or a spare bit set is `certificate does not parse: not base64url`. |
| `refresh_check` | `pin`: `root`: Fingerprint, `endpoint`: string, `leaf`: CertDer, `answer`, `now`: InstantIn | `ok`: true, `fn`: string, `renewed`: `leaf`: CertDer, `spki`: Spki \| null, `root_cert`: CertDer<br>or `ok`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | Refreshing ONE contact's card (SPEC §3, §14.3), the trust decision both hosts made separately (CW-08): what a peer's answer to `get_card` proves about a pinned contact. A refresh can move a leaf and never a root or an address: the chain is validated against the pinned root and the pinned endpoint. The pin is the host's: `pin` absent or null, or not an object, is `pin is required`, a member absent or of the wrong type is `pin.<member> is required` (`pin.leaf` of the wrong type is `parse` `not base64url`), a `pin.root` that is not a fingerprint is `pin.root is not a fingerprint`, judged as the root is read, before `pin.endpoint`, and a pinned leaf that does not read is an error in its reader's class — read before the answer. `answer` absent or null is `answer is required`; then `now`; then the pinned leaf is parsed, and one that is a CA certificate is `bad_request` `pin.leaf is a CA certificate, not a leaf`: the host's pin, never the peer's answer. The answer is then judged in this order, each refusal `{"ok": false, "why"}`: a `card` and a `card_sig` that are non-empty strings (`the answer to get_card carries no signed card`, an answer that is not an object included); a `chain` of exactly two non-empty strings (`the answer carries <n> certificate(s); get_card answers with the chain, leaf then root (§6.1)`, `n` the length of the list, 0 when it is not one); each member base64url (`a chain member is not base64url`); the card decodes at `now` (`the card does not decode: <card_decode's why>`); it names the pinned root (`the card names another root, not the pinned one`); the chain validates at `now` to the pinned root and endpoint (`the chain it answered with fails rule <n>: <reason>`); its leaf is not older than the pinned one (`the leaf it answered with is superseded by the pinned one (§14.3)`) nor another of the same notBefore (`two different leaves claim the same notBefore (§14.3)`); the card carries that leaf (`the card's certificate is not the leaf the chain proved`); `card_sig` is base64url (`the card signature is not base64url`) and verifies over the card's text under the leaf's key, by `verify`'s rules (`the card signature does not verify under the proven leaf key`). |

`card_decode` is intake: it refuses no version, a version it does not implement, zero or several
certificates, a certificate that does not parse, no issuer key identifier or one that is not 32
bytes (it is what `root` is made from, and `root` is what a person is shown), no endpoint or several,
or a validity over 398 days; an expired leaf is reported, not refused. `now` is REQUIRED: it is what
`expired` means, and absent it used to be 1970, so every card answered `expired: false`. The address guard is a separate call
the host makes with its own endpoint in hand.

## 5. Envelopes (SPEC §13)

Suites: `HDTP-SEAL-P256` (DHKEM(P-256, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, AES-128-GCM) for a P-256 recipient,
`HDTP-SEAL-X25519` (DHKEM(X25519, HKDF-SHA256), HKDF-SHA256, ChaCha20-Poly1305) for an Ed25519
recipient converted by the RFC 7748 §4.1 and RFC 8032 §5.1.5 maps; a bare X25519 key is no key of
the profile (§0). A suite that is not the recipient key's is `envelope_invalid`, `suite does not fit
the key`. HPKE Base mode, single shot, `info` = `HDTP-SEAL-v1`. All-zero DH output refused: a seal to
an Ed25519 key of small order meets one, and is `envelope_invalid`, `all-zero DH output: low-order
point`; an open that meets one does not open. The
header is the AAD, canonicalised per RFC 8785; the signature is over `protected ‖ enc ‖ ct`.

**A member of an envelope has ONE spelling** (SPEC §13.1): unpadded base64url, canonical. `decide`
and `open_result` read `protected`, `enc`, `ct` and `sig` with a reader that refuses everything else —
a character outside the alphabet, padding, whitespace, the standard alphabet's `+` and `/`, a last
character with a spare bit set — because `sig` covers the DECODED bytes and every spelling a reader
forgives is another envelope that verifies. This is NOT the rule for an argument a caller hands the
boundary (§0), which stays forgiving about padding and alphabet; it is the rule for what travels.
An unreadable `protected` is `protected is not JSON`, `enc` or `ct` is `does not open`, and a `sig`
that does not read is no signature and fails as one (`open_result`: `signature`).

**A pin MAY say which leaf it holds** (`leaf_fingerprint`). A small-form envelope names a leaf, and
finding the pin that holds it meant parsing every pinned leaf, for a sender who has proved nothing.
With the member, the match is a string comparison and only the pin that matched is parsed; the match
is held to its own leaf (`parse` / `a pin's leaf_fingerprint is not its leaf's`). Without it the pins
are read as before, so an older host loses only the saving. A pin, a held key or a tombstone that
will not read is an ERROR of the call (`parse`), never a row stepped over: a decision made on state
the node could not read is not a decision.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `suite_for` | `spki`: Spki | `suite`: Suite<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |
| `hpke_seal` | `suite`: Suite, `recipient_spki`: Spki, `info`: string, `aad`?: B64url, `plaintext`: B64url, `ephemeral_seed`?: Seed32 | `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` | `ephemeral_seed` exists for vectors and the intrusion suite; production callers omit it and the core draws 32 fresh bytes. `aad` absent is empty. |
| `hpke_open` | `suite`: Suite, `recipient_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `recipient_spki`: Spki, `info`: string, `aad`?: B64url, `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url | `plaintext`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` |  |
| `seal_request` | `recipient_leaf`: CertDer, `sender_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `form`?: Form, `sender_chain`?: Chain, `msg_id`: string, `ts`: integer, `exp`?: integer, `ephemeral_seed`?: Seed32, `method`?: string, `params`?, `cty`?: string | `protected`: B64url, `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url, `sig`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` | `form` absent is `chain`, which needs `sender_chain`; `method` absent is `tools/call`; `params` absent is `{}`; `exp` absent is `ts + 600`; `cty` absent is a call. `params` is sealed as the value it is, not as the text it was written in: strings as RFC 8785 writes them, an integer the core holds as one (an i64, or a u64 past it) by its digits and every other number as RFC 8785 writes it, members in the order they were written, and a member written twice once, where it first appeared, with the value it was given last (as serde_json's ordered map and `JSON.parse` read it; the core's `canonical::in_order`, Go's `inOrder`). Not sorted: Appendix B's plaintexts write `name` before `arguments`. `ts` and `exp` are integers a header carries as themselves, from −(2^53 − 1) to 2^53 − 1: RFC 8785 writes a number as the double it is, so one past that would be sealed as another. `ts` is judged first, then `exp`, the default included, each `bad_request` `<ts|exp> is an integer from -(2^53 - 1) to 2^53 - 1`; both after the members are read (a 31-byte `ephemeral_seed` is named before them) and before the proof member (a chain of one, or none in the chain form, is named after them). |
| `seal_result` | `recipient_spki`: Spki, `sender_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `form`?: Form, `sender_chain`?: Chain, `msg_id`: string, `ts`: integer, `exp`?: integer, `ephemeral_seed`?: Seed32, `result`?, `error`? | `protected`: B64url, `enc`: B64url, `ct`: B64url, `sig`: B64url<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` | Exactly one of `result` and `error`, sealed as `seal_request` seals `params`. `cty` is `application/hdtp-result+json`. `ts` and `exp` (absent: `ts + 600`) are held as `seal_request` holds them, first. |
| `open_result` | `envelope`: ArrivedEnvelope, `my_pkcs8`: Pkcs8, `my_spki`: Spki, `msg_id`: string, `now`: InstantIn, `pins`?: [Pin], `expected_root`?: string, `expected_endpoint`?: string | `ok`: true, `result`?, `error`?, `root`: Fingerprint, `endpoint`: string, `form`: Form, `leaf_update`?: CertDer<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `envelope_invalid`, `parse`, `unsupported` | The caller side of §13.2: opens, requires `result` xor `error` plus one of `chain`/`leaf`, validates the chain to `expected_root` and `expected_endpoint` or finds the named leaf among `pins`, refuses a superseded leaf, verifies `sig`, checks `cty` and `msg_id`. Every refusal of the ENVELOPE is `{"error": "envelope_invalid", "why"}`. `leaf_update` is a leaf newer than the pin, for the host to store. An absent or null `envelope` is the caller's omission, `bad_request` `envelope is required` (CONTRACT §0); a present one is read for its four members in order (`protected`, `enc`, `ct`, `sig`), and one that is not an object, or lacks a member or holds one that is not a string, is `envelope_invalid` naming it (`envelope is required`, `envelope.sig is required`). `pins` absent or null is none; a pin is read for `root`, `endpoint`, `leaf`, `state` and `leaf_fingerprint` in that order, and one that is not an object or lacks a required member, or holds one of the wrong type, is `bad_request` naming it by its path (`pins[0] is required`, `pins[0].root is required`), and a `root` that is not a fingerprint is `pins[<i>].root is not a fingerprint`, a `state` other than the three `pins[<i>].state is active, pending_out or blocked`, and a `leaf_fingerprint` that is not a fingerprint `pins[<i>].leaf_fingerprint is not a fingerprint`, as a node's pin is. A chain in the plaintext with a member that is not a string, or does not read as base64url, is `envelope_invalid` `plaintext shape`, as in `decide`. The first pin for the chain's root is the one read, as `decide` reads a node's pins; a pin whose leaf does not read is an error of the call in its reader's class (`parse`; `unsupported` for a key outside the profile), never `superseded leaf`. |
| `follow_renewed` | `answer`?, `pinned_root`: string, `pinned_leaf`: CertDer, `dialed`: string, `now`: InstantIn | `follow`: true, `leaf`: CertDer<br>or `follow`: false, `why`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | §14.4: `answer` is the peer's `{"code": "certificate_renewed", "data": {"chain"}}`, whatever it actually sent. Validate to the pinned root and the dialed address, and follow only when the chain is newer than or equal to the pin. |
| `decide` | `now`: InstantIn, `envelope`: ArrivedEnvelope, `node`: NodeState | `result`: Decision, `effects`: [Effect]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | §5.1 below. |
| `decide_chain` | `node`: NodeState, `chain`: Chain, `now`: InstantIn | `result`: ChainDecision, `effects`: [PinEffect]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported` | §5.1's pin decision on its own, for a host's TLS door: the part of `decide` after the chain is validated and signed for, written once in each port and taken by both functions, so a chain presented at the TLS layer earns exactly what an envelope carrying it would (N1, N2: the node's TLS door read the removal tombstone in the states `decide` does not, and served a conflicting leaf as a guest). Read as `decide` reads its arguments: `node`, `chain` and `now` absent or null, in that order; the node whole, as `decide` reads it; the chain, as every function reads one (not a list: `chain is required`; a member that is not a base64url string: `parse` `not base64url`); `now`. The chain is validated at `now` with no expectation; one that fails is `envelope_invalid` `chain rule <n>: <reason>`. Then the pins, in `decide`'s order: no pin for the root — a tombstone for it (the first) within 30 days whose leaf the chain's is newer than is `pending_new_address` forced `ask` with a `pending` effect (`returned after removal`), and otherwise a guest (`unknown root`); a blocked pin is a guest (`blocked`); a leaf older than the pinned one a guest (`superseded leaf`); a different leaf of the pinned one's notBefore `envelope_invalid` (`a different leaf with the same notBefore`); another endpoint is `pending_new_address` under `ask` and, under `auto`, a re-pin with the former endpoint recorded and a `new_address` event; a newer leaf at the pinned endpoint a `pin_update` and a `renewal` event; then `pending` for a `pending_out` pin and `contact` otherwise. A guest carries `why`, `demote` and `address_claim`, as `decide`'s does. What is the call's — a guest's tools and card, the receiver's own address (§14.5), what a `pending_out` pin may call — the host applies to each call, as `decide` applies it to the envelope's. There is no `seen`. Node state that does not read is an error of the call in its reader's class, as in `decide`. |

**Plaintext shapes.** A request plaintext is `{"method", "params", "chain" | "leaf"}`. A result
plaintext is `{"result": <object>, "chain" | "leaf"}` or `{"error": {"code", "message", "data"?},
"chain" | "leaf"}` — the responder's proof beside the result, as §13.2 requires; the wrapper is the
clarification this library fixes and Phase 0.5 folds into the spec.

### 5.1 `decide` — the receiving rules as one pure function

`decide` implements SPEC §13.3 in order, §6.1 tiers, §5.3 new addresses with the removal tombstone,
§14.3 and §14.4, over state the host supplies. It changes nothing; it returns what it decided and the
effects the host must apply. `envelope.mjs receive()` is its specification, line for line.

Its arguments are the host's, decoded by the host, so a fault in them fails the call (`bad_request`)
and is never a decision about the peer: `node`, `envelope` and `now` absent or null, in that order
(`<name> is required`); then the node read whole as `NodeState` says, then the envelope's four
members in order, each named by its path when it is absent, null or not the type it is
(`node.pins[0].leaf is required`, `envelope.sig is required`); then `now`.

Input:

```json
{
  "now": "2026-09-13T12:00:00Z",
  "envelope": {"protected": "…", "enc": "…", "ct": "…", "sig": "…"},
  "node": {
    "endpoint": "https://agent.bharat.example/mcp",
    "accept_new_hosts": "auto" | "ask",
    "chain": ["<leaf>", "<root>"],
    "keys": [{"kid": "sha256:…", "leaf": "<leaf der>", "pkcs8": "…", "current": true}],
    "former": ["sha256:…"],
    "sibling_kids": ["sha256:…"],
    "pins": [{"root": "sha256:…", "endpoint": "https://…", "leaf": "<leaf der>", "state": "active" | "pending_out" | "blocked", "leaf_fingerprint"?: "sha256:…"}],
    "tombstones": [{"root": "sha256:…", "leaf": "<leaf der>", "at": "2026-…"}],
    "former_endpoints": [{"root": "sha256:…", "endpoint": "https://…", "at": "2026-…"}],
    "seen": ["msg-id", "…"]
  }
}
```

`keys` are the leaves this endpoint holds for the identity served at the path the envelope arrived
at: the current one and superseded ones the host keeps until their `notAfter` (the core drops a
non-current key past its `notAfter` itself). `former` are the key ids of leaves once held and no
longer, for `certificate_renewed`. `sibling_kids` are the key ids held for *other* identities on the
same origin, so a key held for another identity is `envelope_invalid`, never answered with a chain.

Output:

```json
{
  "result": {"code": "ok", "tier": "contact" | "pending" | "guest" | "pending_new_address",
             "root": "sha256:…", "endpoint": "https://…", "method": "tools/call", "tool": "send_message",
             "params": {…}, "form": "chain" | "leaf", "leaf": "<leaf der the signature verified under>",
             "replayed"?: true, "why"?: "unknown root" | "blocked" | "superseded leaf", "demote"?: false | true,
             "address_claim"?: "sha256:…", "forced"?: "tombstone", "decision"?: "ask"},
  "effects": [
    {"op": "seen", "msg_id": "…"},
    {"op": "pin_update", "root": "…", "endpoint": "…", "leaf": "…"},
    {"op": "former_endpoint", "root": "…", "endpoint": "…", "at": "…"},
    {"op": "event", "event": "new_address" | "renewal", "root": "…", "endpoint"?: "…"},
    {"op": "pending", "root": "…", "endpoint": "…", "leaf": "<leaf der>", "why": "ask" | "returned after removal"}
  ]
}
```

The other results, each with an empty `effects` list unless stated: `{"code": "envelope_invalid",
"why"}` — and when `why` is `guest may only redeem or request` it also carries `root` and `leaf`, so a
host holding an older pin of that leaf's key learns the root above it (§14.3) and decides again; `{"code": "chain_required"}`; `{"code": "certificate_renewed", "data": {"chain": [...]}}`;
`{"code": "pending_approval", "root", "endpoint", "leaf", "form", "msg_id"}` — what the signature
proved and the request's `msg_id`, so a host can seal the refusal back to the caller (§13.2) without
opening the envelope again; its effects are the pin's own moves, never `seen`; and
`{"code": "ok", "replayed": true}` for a seen `msg_id`.
The `why` strings are the seed's, verbatim, so the intrusion suite reads both ports alike.

Order, as `receive()` has it (freshness also refuses `exp − ts` over 30 days, §13.1, as `exp too far from ts`): decode `protected` → header members exactly `cty,exp,kid,msg_id,suite,ts,v`
→ their types (`v`, `ts`, `exp` integers, the rest strings, else `header member types`)
→ `v` = 2 and a known suite → `kid` held (current, or superseded and not past `notAfter`), else a
sibling's → `envelope_invalid`, a former → `certificate_renewed`, unknown → `envelope_invalid` → suite
fits the held leaf's key → `enc` is exactly the suite's `Npk`, 65 or 32 (`encapsulated key is not the suite's length`: `sig` covers the three members concatenated, so the length is what fixes the boundary) → HPKE open → plaintext members exactly `chain,method,params` or
`leaf,method,params`, method `tools/call` or `tools/list` → **small form**: leaf fingerprint matched
against pins not blocked, the held leaf within validity, `sig` verifies, else `chain_required` in every
case; then freshness (`cty` is a call, `now < exp`, `|now − ts| ≤ 300 s`, non-empty `msg_id`, replay) →
tier by pin state → **full form**: `validate_chain` at `now` with no expectation (`envelope_invalid`
with `chain rule N: reason`), `sig` under the chain's leaf key, freshness; root unpinned → tombstone
within 30 days with a newer leaf → `pending_new_address` forced `ask`, else guest; guest binding: the
method is `tools/call`, the tool `redeem_invite` or `request_contact`, `params.arguments.card`
decodes, its certificate byte-equals the chain's leaf, the endpoint is not this node's own
(`guest endpoint is this node's own address`, §14.5), `address_claim` names a pin at that endpoint
or a former endpoint within 30 days; root pinned and blocked → guest; superseded → guest (a guest's
answer carries `why`, one of `unknown root`, `blocked` and `superseded leaf`, and `demote`, true for
the last two: a pin for the root stands and the caller is a guest anyway, so a host resolves it to no
contact row — the host reads `demote`, never the words); conflict →
`envelope_invalid`; another endpoint → `ask` pending or `auto` re-pin with the former endpoint recorded
and a `new_address` event; newer at the pinned endpoint → `pin_update` and a `renewal` event; then
`pending_out` allows `tools/list` and `contact_accepted`/`contact_rejected` at tier `pending` (a listing
names no tool, and answers at the tier the caller earns, SPEC §6, §13.2), else `pending_approval`; else
contact.

A `pending_new_address` result is the host's to answer as SPEC §5.3 words it: the `update_contact` that
brought the new address answers `{"status": "pending"}`; every other call from that address, until the
owner decides, answers `pending_approval`.

`decide_chain` is the same pin decision for a chain proven outside an envelope — at the TLS layer, where
the handshake is the leaf key's signature — so a host's two doors cannot decide one caller two ways
(the node's TLS door did, on a removal tombstone and on a conflicting leaf). Both functions take it
from one place in each port; `js/doors.test.mjs` holds the two answers to each other over every
outcome. What is the call's and not the chain's — the guest binding, the receiver's own address, what
a `pending_out` pin may call — the host applies to each call on its TLS door, as `decide` applies it
to the envelope's.

## 6. Vault (SPEC §9; the format shared by the wallet page and the CLI)

A wallet keeps two sealed documents, and both are this envelope:

```json
{"format": "hdtp-vault/1",
 "kdf": {"name": "argon2id", "m_kib": 65536, "t": 3, "p": 1},
 "salt": "<b64url 16>", "nonce": "<b64url 12>", "ct": "<b64url>"}
```

The key is Argon2id(passphrase, salt) → 32 bytes; the cipher is AES-256-GCM; the AAD is the RFC 8785
canonical JSON of the document without `ct`. The **file** is the root and nothing else — the person's
backup, sealed under the recovery key (in a wallet without a credential, the passphrase the person
chose), written once when the root is made and again only when the root is re-bound or a hardware key
takes it; a wallet never writes a leaf, a ledger entry or a contact into it. A root entry carries its
key (`pkcs8`), names the card that holds it (`holder`), or both — a key imported to a card and kept:

```json
{"v": 1,
 "roots": [{"fingerprint", "cn", "alg"?, "pkcs8"?, "holder"?, "cert", "created"}],
 "prf"?: "<b64url 32: the §2.1 secret, for a derived root>",
 "passkey"?: {"credential_id"}}
```

The **record** is the ledger and the contact book — under the store key of §2.1 for a wallet with a
credential, beside the file under the recovery key for one without — and the roots without their
keys, or with one once a root has been re-bound:

```json
{"v": 1,
 "roots"?: [{"fingerprint", "cn", "cert", "created", "pkcs8"?, "rebound_at"?}],
 "ledger": [{"root", "endpoint", "not_before", "not_after", "issued_at", "origin"?}],
 "contacts": [{"root", "endpoint", "name", "leaf"?, "root_cert"?, "added"}],
 "passkey"?: {"credential_id"}, "backup_verified_at"?: <ms>}
```

A ledger entry is the endpoint and the dates, never the leaf: that is the host's to serve and grants
nothing. `v` is 1 at both ends — `vault_seal` refuses anything else as `bad_request`, and `vault_open`
refuses a document that opens to another generation as `vault` — and nothing converts.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `vault_seal` | `passphrase`: string, `plaintext`, `kdf`?: KdfArgs, `salt`?: B64url, `nonce`?: B64url | `vault`: VaultDocument<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `vault` | `plaintext` is a VaultPlaintext or a RecordPlaintext, and its `v` is 1: anything else is `bad_request` (`a vault plaintext is v 1: the root, or the record`). The plaintext is sealed as `seal_request` seals `params`, as the value it is. That generation is all `vault_seal` checks of the plaintext (and `vault_open` of what it opens): the two shapes are held by `wallet_issue`, where the rules read them, so a stricter seal or open cannot lock a person out of a document a wallet already keeps. Read in this order: `passphrase` (absent: `passphrase is required`; empty: `empty passphrase`), `plaintext` and its generation, then `kdf`, `salt` and `nonce`, then the nonce's length (`vault`, `nonce is 12 bytes`) and the salt's (`vault`, `salt is at least 8 bytes`: `VaultSaltMin`). `kdf` absent or null is `KdfDefault`, and one that is not an object is `bad_request` `kdf is required`. An object is read by the one reader `vault_open` reads a document's `kdf` with, except that a member left out takes the default: a `name` other than `argon2id`, or one that is not a string, is `vault` `unknown kdf`; a parameter that is not a whole number written as one (`1.0`, `-0`, `"8192"`), or is outside its range, is `vault` `kdf parameters out of range`, never truncated; and a member other than those four, named in any case but theirs, is `vault` `kdf holds name, m_kib, t and p, and nothing else: <member>`. `salt` and `nonce` are for tests only. |
| `vault_open` | `passphrase`: string, `vault` | `plaintext`<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `vault` | Read in this order: `vault` (absent or null: `vault is required`), `passphrase` (absent: `passphrase is required`), then the document's header, where it does not read, all `vault`: a document that is not an object, or whose `format` is not `hdtp-vault/1`, is `not an hdtp-vault/1 document`; its `kdf` is read by the one reader `vault_seal`'s is, with all four members (`Kdf`): one that is not an object, or whose `name` is absent, not a string or not `argon2id`, is `unknown kdf`, a parameter that is absent, not a whole number written as one, or outside its range is `kdf parameters out of range`, and another member is `kdf holds name, m_kib, t and p, and nothing else: <member>`; `salt`, `nonce` and `ct` that are absent or not strings are no bytes, and one that is not base64url, or a nonce that is not 12 bytes, is the one message below; then a salt under `VaultSaltMin` bytes is `salt is at least 8 bytes`. A wrong passphrase and a tampered document are one message (`the passphrase is wrong or the vault is damaged`). A document that opens to a plaintext whose `v` is not 1 is of another generation and is refused (`vault`, `this vault is of another generation and is not opened: there is no conversion`); nothing converts. |
| `wallet_issue` | `vault_plaintext`: VaultPlaintext, `record_plaintext`: RecordPlaintext, `root_fingerprint`: string, `csr`: Csr, `now`: InstantIn, `valid_days`?: integer, `move`?: boolean | `der`: CertDer, `endpoint`: string, `not_before`: Instant, `not_after`: Instant, `ledger_entry`: LedgerEntry, `new_host`: boolean, `warnings`: [string]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse`, `unsupported`, `root_expired` | Two documents, as §9 keeps them: the vault is the root and nothing else, the record holds the ledger this reads and the entry answered is appended to. A vault carrying `ledger` or `contacts` is refused (`bad_request`, `a vault holds the root and nothing else: its ledger and contacts belong in the record`); an absent or null document is `vault_plaintext is required` or `record_plaintext is required` (CONTRACT §0), and a record that is not an object `record_plaintext is required: the ledger lives there`. After `root_fingerprint`, `csr`, `now` and `valid_days` (present and not an integer: `valid_days is required`), each document is held to its schema before anything in it is read, as follows. Inside both documents, as in the arguments (CONTRACT §0), a member the document declares that is `null` is absent — an optional one is not there, a required one is named as a missing one is — and a member it does not declare is refused whatever it holds, `null` included (a vault's `ledger: null` is a vault carrying a ledger). The vault: not an object, `vault_plaintext is required: the root lives there`; then its `v`; then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold, `vault_plaintext holds v, roots, prf and passkey, and nothing else: <member>`; then its `roots` (absent or not a list: `the vault's roots is a list`), each entry a `VaultRoot` (`the vault's root <i> does not read: <member>`: the first of `fingerprint`, `cn`, `cert` and `created` that is absent, not a string, not a fingerprint or not an instant, then an `alg`, `pkcs8`, `holder` or `rebound_at` of the wrong type, then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold; an entry that is not an object, `the vault's root <i> does not read`); then its `prf` (32 bytes, or `the vault's prf does not read`) and its `passkey` (an object holding `credential_id`, a string, and nothing else, or `the vault's passkey does not read`). Then the record, likewise: `record_plaintext holds v, roots, ledger, contacts, passkey and backup_verified_at, and nothing else: <member>`; its `roots` where present, as the vault's (`the record's roots is a list`, `the record's root <i> does not read: <member>`); its `ledger` (not a list: `the record's ledger is a list`) and every ledger entry, every root's: an entry that is not an object, lacks a required member, has one of the wrong type, a `root` that is not a fingerprint, an empty `endpoint` or an instant that does not parse, or carries one it does not hold is refused (`the record's ledger entry <i> does not read: <member>`), never skipped — skipped, it could be the live leaf; its `contacts` (not a list: `the record's contacts is a list`), each entry a `VaultContact` (`the record's contact <i> does not read: <member>`: `root` absent or not a fingerprint, `endpoint` absent or not a string, a `name`, `leaf`, `root_cert` or `added` that is not a string or, for `added`, not an instant, then the first member, in sorted order, it does not hold; an entry that is not an object, `the record's contact <i> does not read`); its `passkey` (`the record's passkey does not read`) and its `backup_verified_at`, a whole number (`the record's backup_verified_at does not read`). A root with no `pkcs8` is refused (`this root is held on a card: wallet_issue signs only with a key the vault holds`), and one whose `pkcs8` does not read is refused in its reader's class (`parse`; `unsupported` for a key outside the profile). Then SPEC §2.2, before anything is signed: a root whose entry's `cert` reads and is past its `notAfter` at `now` is refused as `issue_from_csr` refuses it (`root_expired`), before the proof of possession below; the key's fingerprint is `root_fingerprint` (`the vault's root key is not the root it is filed under`); the entry's `cert` reads (in its reader's class) and holds the key (`the vault's root certificate is not its key's`); and the key signs `HDTP root proof v1`, a newline and 32 random bytes, verified under the certificate's key (`the vault's root key does not sign for its certificate`). After issuing, the chain of the leaf and that certificate is validated at `now` against `root_fingerprint` and the request's endpoint before it is answered (`the chain it issued does not validate: chain rule <n>: <reason>`). The entry answered is the endpoint and the dates, never the leaf. The wallet's rules: `csr_check` with the vault's roots as `root_spkis`; then `ledger_check`'s rules over the record's ledger (a record with no `ledger` has no entry to read): `new_host` true when no ledger entry names that endpoint's host, with the warning `new host: this endpoint's host has never been issued to`; the **live leaf is the newest one issued** (§14.3) and a second endpoint while it is unexpired is refused unless `move: true`, which instead warns `move: the live leaf at the previous endpoint is superseded once contacts see this one` (a `move` or a `move_back`); `not_before` monotonic over the ledger; `valid_days` absent means 365 and an explicit 0 is refused. A leaf ends no later than its root, and `warnings` then carries `issue_from_csr`'s line saying so. |

Passphrases never appear in arguments of the CLI; the wallet page holds them in memory
only for the call, and an empty passphrase seals nothing (`bad_request`). What the core zeroizes
when a call returns: every private key it decoded, the PKCS #8 bytes it decoded them from, the
HPKE ephemeral, shared secret, key, nonce and the HMAC chaining buffers, the vault's derived key
and its decrypted bytes. What it does not: the JSON argument and answer strings — including a
`pkcs8` member and a vault's decoded plaintext as a JSON value — and wasm-bindgen's copies of
those strings in linear memory, which are freed but not cleared. A host that must not leave key
material behind treats the strings it passes and receives as its own to clear.

**The KDF's range, at both ends, on both paths.** `m_kib` 8192–2097152 (8 MiB–2 GiB), `t` 1–16, `p` 1–16, `name` `argon2id`; anything else is `{"error": "vault", "why": "kdf parameters out of range"}` (or `"unknown kdf"`), from `vault_seal` and `vault_open` alike, through one reader in each port, and every derivation — a typed call's too — is held to the same range. The parameters are read out of the document **before the passphrase is tested**, so an unbounded reader hands an attacker's file a 256 GiB allocation or a derivation that never returns, and an unbounded writer seals the person's root behind a KDF a laptop brute-forces. A value that does not fit in 32 bits is out of range, never truncated. A salt under `VaultSaltMin` (8 bytes) is `{"error": "vault", "why": "salt is at least 8 bytes"}` at both ends, named before Argon2id is asked for anything: no `why` is the library's.

### 6.1 The ledger — what signing would mean

`ledger_check` is SPEC §9's issuance rules over the record's ledger, answered as facts and not as
prose: whether a leaf is live and where, whether this endpoint or its host has been issued to, the
`notBefore` the next leaf must follow, and which move notice applies (`renew`, `move`, `new_host`,
`move_back`, or `no_ledger` when the signer has no record to read). `wallet_issue` applies these
rules; the `hdtp` CLI applies them to a card-held root, where there is no key to hand the core; a
wallet page and a host render the notice from them. Every entry is read before any rule is, and one
that does not read is refused, never skipped.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ledger_check` | `ledger`?: array\|null, `root`: Fingerprint, `endpoint`: string, `now`: InstantIn, `move`?: boolean | `refusal`: string\|null, `new_host`: boolean, `known_endpoint`: boolean, `previous_not_before`: Instant \| null, `live`: `endpoint`: string, `not_after`: Instant \| null, `notice`: `kind`: renew\|move\|new_host\|move_back\|no_ledger, `from`?: string, `until`?: Instant<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | The wallet's ledger rules, as facts, in the one place they are written: `wallet_issue` applies them, the `hdtp` CLI applies them for a card-held root, and a wallet page or a host renders the move notice from them. In order: `root` (absent or empty: `root is required`), `endpoint`, `now`, `move` (present and not a boolean: `move is required`); then `endpoint` not in normal form is refused (`endpoint is not an https URL in normal form`); then every ledger entry, every root's, is read as `wallet_issue` reads it (`the record's ledger is a list`; `the record's ledger entry <i> does not read: <member>`, a `root` that is not a fingerprint and an empty `endpoint` included) — an entry that does not read is REFUSED, a `not_before` that does not parse included, never skipped: skipped, it could be the live leaf. The **live leaf** is this root's newest entry by `not_before` (§14.3; the first of equals, in ledger order), if its `not_after` is after `now`; an older entry still in its validity is history, not live. `notice.kind`: with no ledger, `no_ledger`; a leaf live at another endpoint, `move_back` when this endpoint has been issued to before and `move` when it has not (both with `from` and `until`, the live leaf's endpoint and `not_after`); otherwise `renew` when this endpoint has been issued to, and `new_host` when it has not. The kind does not depend on `move`; only `refusal` does. |

### 6.2 The export (SPEC §9.2)

An export is one unencrypted zip — `manifest.json`, `contacts.csv`, `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl`,
`media/<sha256>` — and a wallet's book is one holding the manifest and `contacts.csv` only. The core
never opens a zip: a host reads the container and hands over what it read, and every rule that can
be decided on that is decided here, once. Every refusal of what a file holds, or of rows to write,
is `bad_request`, and its `why` begins with where: the member, then the row (the header is row 1) or
the line, then the column or member. An argument that is not an instant (`now`, `exported_at`) is
`parse`, as everywhere in this contract.

**Reading.** The host passes `export_read` the central directory and the three text members, then
streams `messages.jsonl` through `export_read_messages` in batches of lines (`first_line` numbering
them in the whole member), then checks each media file, then calls `export_read_end`. What only
the host can do, and the words both hosts of this repository use for it (the Go port's
`ReadExportZip` and the `hdtp` CLI):

- count the bytes it actually decompresses, never the sizes a header states: a text member over its
  bound is `<member>: over <n> bytes`, a line `messages.jsonl: line <n>: over 65536 bytes`, a media
  file `media/<h>: over 5242880 bytes`, and the whole file over the host's own ceiling `the file is
  over the <n>-byte ceiling this host sets`;
- refuse a member that is not UTF-8 text (`<member>: not UTF-8 text`, or `messages.jsonl: line <n>:
  not UTF-8 text`) and one that does not decompress (`<member>: does not decompress`);
- hash `messages.jsonl` as it streams it, and each media file against its own name (`media/<h>: its
  sha256 is not its name`): the manifest lists the text members only, and a media member is bound
  by its name and counted by `counts.media`;
- refuse a media file whose bytes are a private key — PKCS #8 or SEC1 in DER, or text holding one
  (`media/<h>: holds a private key`) — which it asks `media_holds_private_key`, the rule both ports'
  readers apply, rather than keep a copy of it;
- hand `export_read_end` the media `export_read` answered, so a media file no message names is
  refused.

**Writing.** `export_write` answers the canonical `contacts.csv` and `threads.csv` and a partial
manifest; `export_write_messages` answers the lines; `export_manifest` finishes the manifest with
the host's count and hash of `messages.jsonl`. The bytes are the same from every port: a Go host and
a Rust host that write the same rows write the same file. A media file is stored, not recompressed.
What a contact controls never stops the export (SPEC 9.2#22–25): `export_write_messages` leaves out
a message whose body is a private key and answers it in `left_out`, and a host that writes in
batches names the file's msg_ids in `msg_ids`, so a reply to a message not carried is written null.
The core never sees a media file's bytes unless it is handed them, so the host checks each before it
writes, with `media_holds_private_key`: a message whose file is a private key is left out with the file
and listed with the rest, for the host to report to the person.
`book_rows` is the one mapping from the wallet's own book (`VaultContact`, §6) to those rows, which
every wallet uses before `export_write` writes a book.

The Go port also offers two conveniences over these functions, which are not contract functions and
which its own tests run against the whole corpus: `ReadExportZip` (the reading above, with
`archive/zip`) and `WriteExportZip`, which runs the reader's rules on what it is handed before it
writes the first byte. The fixture corpus is `go/exportcorpus/`: two valid exports (one whose local
headers disagree with its central directory), a valid book, and hostile files, each naming the
refusal it must produce (`go/exportcorpus/cases.json`); both ports' tests and `js/parity.mjs` read
all of it. Its files name one fixed owner; `hdtp vectors corpus --owner <root> --out <dir>` writes
the same corpus for another root, each file with its defect and `cases.json` with the same
refusals, so a host can import every file into an identity it holds. Read-side parity cases on the core's functions (`js/cases/export-reader.mjs`) reach
rules that no file does.

| Function | Input | Output | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `export_read` | `directory`: [DirectoryEntry], `manifest`?: string, `contacts_csv`?: string, `threads_csv`?: string, `owner`: Fingerprint, `now`: InstantIn | `contacts`: [ContactRow], `threads`: [ThreadRow], `media`: [`hash`: Sha256Hex, `size`: integer]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | SPEC §9.2's validation of everything but the messages and the media bytes, refusing the whole file at the first fault; every refusal of the file is `bad_request` whose `why` names the member, then the row (the header is row 1) and the column. In order: each directory entry, in the order given (a name that is not exactly `manifest.json`, `contacts.csv`, `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl`, `media/` or `media/` and 64 lowercase hex: `entry "<name>": not a name an export holds`; `appears twice`; `encrypted`; a symbolic link; a directory but `media/`; a stated size over its bound); `manifest.json` and `contacts.csv` present; the manifest (exactly its members, `hdtp_export` 1, `owner` a fingerprint and the importing identity's, the counts whole numbers, `owner_name` and `tool` holding no private key, `files` naming only the text members — `contacts.csv`, `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl` — each a lowercase hex sha256, never a media member, which is bound by its name and counted); every text member but the manifest listed in `files`, and every listed member present; `threads.csv`, `messages.jsonl` and `media/` present when counted; the media entries as many as counted; `contacts.csv` (its sha256, its header exactly, at most 5000 rows, each row's cells — a cell that holds a private key is refused before its column's rule — the root a fingerprint, unique, not the owner; the endpoint in normal form and passing the address guard; names at most 200 characters; the status; `true` or `false`; §8's permissions, single-spaced, none twice; the leaf a leaf and the root certificate a root of §14.1's profile, the latter for the row's root; `added` an instant) and its count; then `threads.csv` the same way, under one of two headers: `id,contact,topic,created_at,last_at`, where every contact is a root in `contacts.csv` (`names no contact in contacts.csv`), or that and `contact_name,contact_display_name`, when the file holds a removed thread: a thread whose contact is no root of `contacts.csv`, a fingerprint and not the owner, its names at most 200 characters and the same on every removed thread of that root (`not what an earlier removed thread of this contact says`), while any other thread's names are empty; the longer header with no removed thread is refused (`threads.csv: row 1: the header names contact_name and contact_display_name, and no thread is a removed thread`). A header that is neither is refused naming both (`threads.csv: row 1: the header is not id,contact,topic,created_at,last_at, nor that and contact_name,contact_display_name`). Ids are unique. A removed thread is answered with its two names, any other thread without them. Before either CSV member is parsed, a member holding more than 65536 characters below U+0020 but tab, line feed and carriage return is refused (`<member>: <n> characters below U+0020 but tab, line feed and carriage return, over the 65536 this library takes in one member`): this library's ceiling, as a host's own (SPEC §9.2), since each is six bytes in this answer. One leading `'` is stripped from every cell. A row's `leaf` is answered only when `[leaf, root_cert]` validates at the row's endpoint at `now` (§14.2); otherwise it is null and pins nothing. `media` is each media member's hash and stated size, sorted by hash: the host checks each file's bytes against both as it streams it. |
| `export_read_messages` | `lines`: [string], `threads`: [string], `contacts`: [Fingerprint], `media`: [Sha256Hex], `first_line`?: integer | `messages`: [MessageRow], `media_seen`: [Sha256Hex]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | One batch of messages.jsonl's lines as the host streams it (each line without its `\n`). Each line: at most 65536 bytes, one JSON object, exactly the members of a message (a stranger first, then a missing one), no member holding a private key, then each member's rule: `id` and `msg_id` not empty, `thread` and `contact` naming the file's, `direction`, `sender`, `time`, `body` at most 16384 bytes, `reply_to` a msg_id or null, `status`, and `attachments` at most one, each exactly `{file, filename, mime, size}` naming a media member; a message with an attachment has an empty body. A refusal is `messages.jsonl: line <n>, member <m>: <why>`. What only the whole member can decide is export_read_end's. |
| `export_read_end` | `manifest`: string, `messages_sha256`?: Sha256Hex \| null, `lines`: integer, `ids`: [string], `msg_ids`: [string], `reply_tos`: [string], `media_seen`: [Sha256Hex], `media`: [Sha256Hex] | `ok`: true<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | SPEC §9.2's rules across the whole of messages.jsonl, once it is streamed: the line count against `counts.messages`, the member's sha256 against `files`, `id` unique in the file, every `reply_to` naming a `msg_id` in the file, and every media member (`media`, the hashes export_read answered) named by some attachment (`media/<h>: nothing names it`). `lines` absent or null is `lines is required`, and one that is not a whole number `lines is a whole number`. |
| `export_write` | `owner`: Fingerprint, `owner_name`: string, `exported_at`: InstantIn, `tool`: string, `contacts`: [ContactRow], `threads`?: [ThreadRow], `media`?: [`hash`: Sha256Hex, `size`: integer] | `partial`: ExportManifest, `contacts_csv`: string, `threads_csv`: string\|null<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | The canonical members, the same bytes from every port: each row checked by the reader's rules (`contacts[<i>], column <c>: <why>`), contacts sorted by root and threads by id, a permission list sorted, instants written as RFC 3339 UTC seconds, every cell that begins with `=` `+` `-` `@` `'` a tab or a carriage return written with one `'` before it, a cell quoted exactly when it holds `,` `"` CR or LF, CRLF after every record. What a contact controls never stops the export (SPEC §9.2): every name (`name`, `display_name`, `contact_name`, `contact_display_name`) and a thread's `topic` lose every character below U+0020 but tab, line feed and carriage return, before a name's length is checked; an `id` is written as given, so a host that takes a thread id holding them may write a file the reader's ceiling refuses; `their_permissions` keeps only the names of §8, once each, and `display_name`, a contact's or a removed thread's `contact_display_name`, is cut to 200 characters, on a character; the reader refuses both as written by anyone else. A thread whose contact is no contact is a removed thread and carries its former contact's names, the same on every thread of that root (`threads[<i>], column contact_name: not what an earlier removed thread of this contact says`); non-empty names on any other thread are refused. `threads_csv` has the longer header, with `contact_name,contact_display_name`, only when a removed thread is among the threads: every other file is the file a writer without removed threads writes. `owner_name` or `tool` holding a private key is refused, naming the member (`owner_name holds a private key`). The manifest's `files` lists the text members only; the media are counted. A book is this with no threads and no media. |
| `export_write_messages` | `messages`: [MessageRow], `msg_ids`?: [string] | `lines`: [string], `left_out`: [`id`: string, `reason`: string]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | One line per message, in the order given, as RFC 8785 JSON; each message held to the reader's rules but its references, which the host holds (`messages[<i>], member <m>: <why>`). What a contact controls never stops the export (SPEC §9.2): a message whose `body` holds what reads as a private key is left out, not refused, and listed in `left_out` (`its body holds what reads as a private key, which an export never carries`) — the host leaves out the file it carried too; and a `reply_to` naming a message the file does not carry (not among `msg_ids`, or, without them, not among the messages written) is written `null`. Key material in any other member is refused. The host writes each line followed by `\n`, hashes the member's bytes and counts its lines for export_manifest. |
| `export_manifest` | `partial`: ExportManifest, `hashes`?: `messages.jsonl`?: Sha256Hex, `messages`?: integer | `manifest`: string<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | export_write's partial manifest finished with what the host counted and hashed: held to the manifest's rules first, refused if it already counts or lists messages, `messages.jsonl` required in `hashes` when there are messages. |
| `export_merge` | `held`: [ContactRow], `rows`: [ContactRow] | `write`: [ContactRow], `keep`: [Fingerprint], `conflicts`: [`root`: Fingerprint, `field`: endpoint\|leaf\|root_cert\|status\|permissions, `held`, `row`]<br>*fails:* `bad_request` | SPEC §9.2's import step 2: an imported leaf never replaces a pin the host validated itself (§14.5). A row whose root is not held is written; a row whose root is held WITHOUT a leaf is written when the row carries one (export_read kept it only because it validated); and what the person decided about that contact stays as held: a blocked contact stays blocked, and its `permissions` stay the ones granted. Every other held root is kept as held. Each of the endpoint, leaf and root certificate a row would change, and each of the `status` and `permissions` (a list compared as a set), is a conflict for the host to show. A held row or a row is refused, `bad_request` naming it, for a `root` that is not a fingerprint (`held[<i>]: root is not a fingerprint`), a `status` other than the three (`rows[<i>]: status is not active, blocked or pending_out`: a held `Blocked` was read as not blocked, so the import did not keep the block) and an `added` that is not an instant (`held[<i>]: added is not an RFC 3339 instant`), export_read's words; the rows' other members are read for what the merge needs. |
| `book_rows` | `contacts`: [VaultContact], `exported_at`: InstantIn | `rows`: [ContactRow]<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | The wallet's book as rows of contacts.csv, the one mapping every wallet uses (SPEC §9.2: a book is an export of contacts only). Each contact, in order: an object (`contacts[<i>] is an object`), no member but `root`, `endpoint`, `name`, `leaf`, `root_cert` and `added` (the first other, in sorted order: `contacts[<i>]: "<m>" is not a member of a wallet contact`), `root` and `endpoint` strings (`contacts[<i>]: <m> is required`), the rest strings when present (`contacts[<i>]: <m> is a string`), then a `root` that is a fingerprint (`contacts[<i>]: root is not a fingerprint`) and an `added`, when present, that is an instant (`contacts[<i>]: added is not an RFC 3339 instant`): both reach the row as its root and its `added`, which the contract types. A row carries the root, the endpoint, the name (empty when absent), the leaf and the root certificate (null when absent), and `added` (the export's time when absent); its other columns are what a contact the wallet keeps is: an empty `display_name`, `status` `active`, `was_active` true, and nothing granted either way. The rows are not otherwise checked here: export_write holds each to the reader's rules. |
| `media_holds_private_key` | `bytes`: B64url | `holds_private_key`: boolean<br>*fails:* `bad_request`, `parse` | SPEC §9.2's key material over a media file, the check CONTRACT §6.2 leaves to a host because the core never sees a file: every port's export reader judges a media file by it, and a host that streams media asks it here rather than keeping a copy. It reads leniently, as a lenient decoder would: a word forgives its padding, either alphabet and a last character whose spare bits are set, and a DER length may take any definite form of up to four octets, minimal or not, so that nothing a person's tools read as a key is passed as none. `js/key-material.json` is the list of cases. |

### 6.3 The call budgets (SPEC §12)

SPEC §12's per-caller budgets as one decision, for the check a host runs after it has opened an
envelope and knows the caller (layer 2 of hdtp-gateway `docs/release/two-layer-limits-2026-09-28.md`;
layer 1, per address and per path, is the host's edge). The rules are a document the host keeps in
its configuration and checks with `limits_rules_check` before it publishes one; the library holds no
default. The counters are rows the host keeps, handed in as `state` and handed back as `writes`: the
library does no I/O and reads no clock. `limits_buckets` names the rows a charge reads, with each
bucket's rate and burst, so a host fetches them from the key scheme written here and not from a copy
of it. A call is charged to every bucket of its charge or to none,
and the bucket keys are the cloud's `rate_buckets` keys, so rows written before the move read the
same after it. The arithmetic is what the cloud's `RateLimiter.take` was, operation for operation,
